title: Investigatio motuum, quibus laminae et virgae elasticae contremiscunt

deep.reconstruction:
Context: E526 sets up Euler-Bernoulli transverse vibrations of an elastic rod. Each mode has the form y = v(x)·sin(nt), with v'''' = (ω/a)^4·v. On each span, v is a combination of e^{±ωx/a}, sin(ωx/a) and cos(ωx/a); a is the total length. On the previous page Euler treats a rod EF pinned ('stylo fixa') at both ends and at an intermediate point L, with EL = λa. Matching deflection, slope and moment at L gives a determinantal frequency equation: 0 = 2 − 2e^{2ω} − (e^{λω} − e^{(2−λ)ω})(e^{λω} − e^{−λω})·sin ω / (sin λω · sin(1−λ)ω). He declines to solve it for general λ and turns to the midpoint support, λ = 1/2.

This page, §48: with λ = 1/2 the product (e^{ω/2} − e^{3ω/2})(e^{ω/2} − e^{−ω/2}) equals −(e^ω − 1)^2 = (1 − e^ω)(e^ω − 1). Clearing sin^2(ω/2) gives 0 = 2(1 − e^{2ω})·sin^2(ω/2) − (1 − e^ω)(e^ω − 1)·sin ω. He removes the trivial factor 1 − e^ω, which gives ω = 0, the state of rest. Writing sin ω = 2 sin(ω/2)cos(ω/2), the equation factors as sin(ω/2)·[(1 + e^ω)·sin(ω/2) − (e^ω − 1)·cos(ω/2)] = 0.

In modern terms these are the two mode families of a symmetric two-span continuous beam:
(i) sin(ω/2) = 0, i.e. ω = 2iπ. These are antisymmetric modes: each half vibrates as a simply supported beam of length a/2, with zero moment at the middle support.
(ii) tan(ω/2) = (e^ω − 1)/(e^ω + 1) = tanh(ω/2). These are symmetric modes: zero slope at the middle support, so each half acts as a clamped-pinned beam of length a/2.

§49 begins case (i). Euler identifies it with his earlier 'casus quartus' (pinned-pinned) with ω replaced by ω/2. On the next page he concludes the tones are two octaves higher, because frequency scales as 1/length^2. He then computes the mode coefficients, handling the 0/0 forms by multiplying through by sin(ω/2).
errors: No mathematical error on this page; every reduction checks.
Minor: 'sin.½ω²' denotes sin²(½ω), in Euler's usual notation.
Minor gap: the parenthetical says the factor 1 − e^ω yields only ω = 0. That holds for real ω, which suffices here.
Minor gap: the excluded root ω = 0 of the sin(ω/2) factor is not explicitly discarded at this point.

ideas.what: Frequency equation of a beam simply supported at both ends with an intermediate support. Specialised to a midpoint support, it factors into sin(ω/2) = 0 and tan(ω/2) = tanh(ω/2).
ideas.modern_name: Free vibration of a two-span continuous Euler-Bernoulli beam; decomposition into symmetric and antisymmetric modes
ideas.usually_credited_to: Euler, E526 (discussed by Truesdell 1960); the continuous-beam theory itself is credited to 19th-century engineering (Clapeyron's three-moment equation for statics; later Rayleigh and others for vibrations)
ideas.where_published: E526, Novi Commentarii / Acta Acad. Petrop. 1779 (published 1782); Opera omnia II.11; reviewed in Truesdell, The Rational Mechanics of Flexible or Elastic Bodies (OO II.11.2)

ideas.what: Antisymmetric modes coincide with pinned-pinned modes of a half-length rod, with tones raised by two octaves.
ideas.modern_name: Frequency scaling ω ∝ L^{-2} for beams; mode reduction by symmetry
ideas.where_published: E526; frequency scaling already in E65 (1744) and D. Bernoulli's papers of 1742–1751

ideas.what: Symmetric modes governed by tan(ω/2) = tanh(ω/2), the clamped-pinned equation for a half-length rod.
ideas.modern_name: Clamped-pinned beam characteristic equation tan βL = tanh βL
ideas.where_published: E526 (earlier case of the same paper, presumably); unsure about other texts

deep.surprise_reason: This is a correct, routine specialisation of the two-span beam frequency equation into symmetric and antisymmetric families. E526, including the intermediate-support case, is covered in Opera omnia and in Truesdell's survey. Nothing on this page appears to be absent from the record.
transcription_corrections: 'sin.½ω²' should be read as sin²(½ω); in the first equation the denominator is sin²(½ω).
The transcription is otherwise faithful to the image (e.g. 2 − 2e^{2ω}, (e^{½ω} − e^{3/2 ω})(e^{½ω} − e^{−½ω})).
